transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose... I mean, my associates suggested I come in, but honestly, I’m here because I just feel this overwhelming sense that I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. You know, patients come in, they look at you with that expectation that you have all the answers, and lately, I just... I can't shake the feeling that I'm completely failing them. I keep replaying these tiny, almost insignificant clinical interactions in my head—like, maybe I didn't explain a medication side effect thoroughly enough, or I hesitated for a second while reading a lab result. Small things, things that my colleagues wouldn't even think twice about, but for me, they just loop endlessly. And every time I replay them, they feel heavier, like they're absolute proof that I'm a dangerous doctor. I just sit there at night, going over and over these moments, convincing myself that it's only a matter of time before I cause real harm. It's exhausting, and I just can't seem to turn it off, no matter how much I try to rationalize it. It's like this constant weight, this guilt that I'm somehow a fraud and a risk to the very people I'm supposed to be helping.
Do you find yourself having repetitive, intrusive thoughts that you try to suppress or ignore?

Suppress them? No... no, I wouldn't say I try to suppress or ignore them at all. I know I just said a moment ago that I wish I could turn it off because it’s so incredibly exhausting, but it’s not like I’m actively fighting to push the thoughts out of my mind. It’s actually quite the opposite, to be completely honest with you. 

When the thought hits me—say, the idea that I completely mismanaged a basic hypertension follow-up or missed a subtle lab abnormality—I don't ignore it. I feel like I *have* to think about it. I feel this intense, almost moral obligation to sit there and dissect every single second of that appointment. I’ll sit on the edge of my bed for hours, just staring at the floor, replaying the exact words I used, wondering if my tone was dismissive, or if I missed a sign of something much worse. 

It’s not like some bizarre, random thought popping into my head out of nowhere that I have to bat away. It’s just this heavy, undeniable truth that I’m doing harm. So, no, I don't suppress them. If anything, I lean into them, because if I were to just ignore those thoughts, wouldn't that just make me an even more negligent doctor? A responsible physician is supposed to reflect on their shortcomings, right? So I just let the thoughts play out, over and over, analyzing every detail, even though it completely drains whatever energy I have left for the day. I just... I feel like I deserve to feel awful about it, because it's my fault, so ignoring it isn't really an option for me.
Do you believe these thoughts about being a bad doctor are true, or do they feel foreign to you?

Foreign? No... no, they don't feel foreign at all. Honestly, they feel like the absolute truth. It’s not like some strange, alien idea that just popped into my head from nowhere. It feels like I’m the only one who is actually seeing reality for what it is. 

I mean, I will literally go back into the electronic medical record system—sometimes late at night or on my days off, which I know my associates would tell me is a terrible habit, but I just can't stop myself—and I'll review the charts. I’ll go through every single line of a patient's history, the nursing notes, the lab trends, the exact timestamps of when I placed an order. And the thing is... even when I review the chart and there’s absolutely no evidence of a bad outcome—like, the patient’s blood pressure is perfectly controlled, or their post-op recovery is completely unremarkable—I still just *know* I've done something terrible. 

I look at the screen, and instead of feeling relieved that they are fine, I keep believing that some routine delay on my part, or some slightly imperfect message I sent to the triage nurse, has quietly harmed them. Like, maybe I took three hours to respond to a non-urgent portal message instead of one, or my phrasing in a consult note wasn't explicit enough, and because of that, I've set off this invisible, irreversible chain reaction of harm. The fact that the chart looks fine right now doesn't comfort me; it just tells me that the damage hasn't surfaced yet. It’s brewing underneath. And I just live with this absolute certainty that everyone will eventually discover it. I'm just waiting for the morbidity and mortality conference to be called, or for the chief of staff to pull me aside, or the medical board to notify me. The proof is going to come out, and they're all going to see that I’ve been quietly damaging these people who trusted me. So, no, they don't feel foreign at all. They feel incredibly real, and I'm just waiting for everyone else to catch up to what I already know I've done.
Do you think these thoughts about being a bad doctor are in line with your own self-image and how you want to be as a doctor?

In line with how I want to be? Well... no, I mean, obviously not. I don't think anyone goes into medicine *wanting* to be a bad doctor. When I started medical school, you know, back when I was just so eager and naive, I had this whole vision of the kind of physician I was going to be. I wanted to be meticulous, compassionate, the kind of doctor who catches the things everyone else misses. I spent years in residency practically killing myself to build this image of being the reliable one. You know, the guy the attendings could always trust to know a patient's exact sodium level from three days ago, the one the interns could look up to when the floors got chaotic. That was always my goal. So, no, feeling like I'm constantly on the verge of causing irreparable harm is definitely not how I *want* to be. 

But... as for my actual self-image right now? I'm not really sure how to separate the two anymore. I guess... I guess my self-image has just completely morphed into this person who fails. It’s like, when I wake up and I'm standing in front of the bathroom mirror before I put my badge on for the day, I don't see that reliable, competent guy anymore. I just see a massive liability. I see someone who is essentially just playing dress-up in a clinic, just waiting for the other shoe to drop. 

So it completely contradicts everything I ever wanted to be, everything I sacrificed my twenties to train for, but at the exact same time... it is exactly who I feel I am right now. It's who I *know* I am. I'm not sure if that really answers your question, or if I'm even making sense, but it's just this massive disconnect between the oath I took and the reality of the damage I feel like I'm doing every single time I log into the system. My associates, they still look at me like I'm that same capable guy from residency, and it just makes the guilt so much worse because I know I'm not him anymore. I'm just... I'm just this hazard they haven't caught yet.
Do you think these thoughts about being a bad doctor are something that you would consider as a part of yourself?

Part of myself? I mean... I don't know if I'd use those exact words, but I guess, in a way, yes. It’s hard to explain without sounding completely unhinged, but it’s like... they aren't just thoughts anymore. They aren't just these fleeting worries that pass through my mind while I'm driving home or waiting in line for coffee. They feel like they've actually seeped into my bones. 

I remember back when I was an intern, if I made a mistake—like, say I forgot to check a morning potassium level or I was late putting in a discharge summary—I would feel bad, sure. I’d beat myself up for a day, maybe two, but then I'd learn from it, right? I'd tell myself, "Okay, you messed up, but you're still a good doctor, you're just learning." The thought of being a bad doctor was something outside of me, something I was actively fighting against. 

But now? Now it doesn't feel like something outside of me at all. It feels like it's the core of who I am. When I think about the fact that I'm harming these patients, it doesn't feel like a symptom or a fear. It feels like a fundamental truth about my character. It’s like... if you were to strip away the white coat, the stethoscope, the diploma on the wall in my office... all that's left underneath is this profound, undeniable incompetence. 

So, yes, I suppose I do consider it a part of myself. It’s not a part I want, obviously. I hate it. It makes every single interaction I have—with patients, with my associates, even with the nurses at the station—feel like a complete fraud. I sit there nodding, pretending I know what I'm doing, but inside, I just know that I am inherently, intrinsically, a danger to them. It’s not just something I think; it’s something I am. Does that make sense? It’s just... it’s completely taken over how I view myself as a human being, not just as a physician.
Do you feel like these thoughts of being a bad doctor are consistent with your own values and beliefs about yourself?

Values... I mean, when you talk about values, the very first thing that comes to mind is the oath, right? "First, do no harm." That is the foundational value of my entire adult life. I built my whole moral compass around patient safety, around being a meticulous, caring provider. So, in one sense, these thoughts about being a terrible, dangerous physician are the exact opposite of what I value. They represent my absolute worst nightmare. I value competence, I value vigilance, and I value integrity. 

But... if you're asking about my *beliefs* about myself, about what I actually believe to be true right now? Then, yes. Yes, they are completely consistent with what I believe about myself, because I firmly believe I have failed all of those values. I know I touched on this a minute ago, but it's just so consuming... it's why I can't stop obsessing over the records. Even when I review the chart and there’s absolutely no evidence of a bad outcome—like, the patient is discharged, they are at home, their labs are stone-cold normal—I still keep believing that some routine delay on my part, or some slightly imperfect message I sent to the floor nurses, has quietly harmed them. 

It’s like my brain completely bypasses the objective data. I’ll see a perfectly stable patient, but because I know I took an extra twenty minutes to respond to a page because I was tied up, or because my phrasing in a handoff wasn't flawlessly precise, I believe with every fiber of my being that I've set a tragedy in motion. I've violated my core value of doing no harm, even if the harm is invisible right now. And because I value honesty, the fact that I'm just sitting here, going to work every day while this quiet damage is out there... it feels like a massive betrayal. I'm just carrying around this heavy, sinking belief that it's all going to catch up to me, and that everyone will eventually discover exactly how much I've failed these people. 

So it’s this horrible paradox. The thoughts are completely opposed to the values I hold dear, but they perfectly match the belief I have that I am, at my core, a failure who has irreparably compromised those values. I don't know if that distinction makes sense to anyone but me, but it’s just how my mind is processing everything right now. I just can't shake the belief that I'm a walking violation of everything I ever stood for.
Are these thoughts about being a bad doctor affecting your ability to perform your daily tasks or responsibilities outside of work?

Well, affecting my tasks... yes. Yes, it really is. I mean, I’m still showing up to the clinic every day. I still put on the clothes, grab my badge, and drive the exact same route I always take, because that routine is just so ingrained in me. I physically get there. But once I'm there... it’s like wading through wet cement. It’s definitely started to affect how reliably I function. The clinical side takes absolutely everything out of me because I'm obsessing and double-checking myself, which leaves zero capacity for anything else. I’ve actually had to ask for help with the non-urgent administrative work, which is incredibly embarrassing for me. Usually, I'm the one who handles the clinic's monthly scheduling, the committee emails, the endless insurance prior authorizations without even blinking. But last week, I had to ask one of my associates to take all of that over. I just stared at the spreadsheets and felt this overwhelming dread, like if I made one wrong keystroke on a schedule or an email, it would cascade into some massive disaster. I just couldn't do it.

And then outside of work? It’s even worse. You asked about responsibilities outside of work, and honestly, just maintaining a basic human life feels completely impossible right now. I completely avoid social plans. It’s not just that I don't have the energy—though, honestly, my energy is completely shot; by the time I get home, I just collapse on the couch in my scrubs and stare at the wall—but it's more about the fact that I just don't trust my own judgment anymore. About anything. 

If I can't even trust myself to evaluate a patient safely, how can I trust myself to go out to dinner and be a normal, functioning friend? I had a few buddies from my residency cohort invite me out for a birthday thing this past weekend, and I just made up some excuse about being on call. I couldn't bear the thought of sitting there at a restaurant, trying to make small talk, knowing what a danger I am to my patients. It felt wrong to even pretend to be normal. I feel so incredibly disconnected from everyone outside of the hospital. So, yeah, it's bleeding into absolutely everything. It’s affecting how reliably I function at work, and it's completely destroyed how connected I am outside of it. I just don't have the capacity or the trust in myself to engage with my own life anymore.
Are these thoughts about being a bad doctor causing you significant emotional distress?

Distress... yeah. Significant doesn't even really begin to cover it, honestly. It’s more like... it's like this constant, suffocating weight. I wake up in the morning, and before I even open my eyes, before my brain even fully registers that I'm awake or what day it is, there's this immediate, crushing sense of dread. It just sits right right on my chest, this heavy, physical ache. 

I just lie there staring at the ceiling, and the loop just instantly starts up. The thoughts just start playing on repeat—that I'm a fraud, that I'm hurting people, that I'm dangerous. And the emotional toll of that, the actual distress... I mean, I've had moments recently where I'm just sitting in my car in the clinic parking garage before my shift, gripping the steering wheel so hard my hands are cramping, and I'm just sobbing. I haven't cried like this since... well, I don't even know if I've ever cried like this in my entire life. It's this profound, agonizing guilt that just gnaws at me every single second of the day. 

And it’s not just a fleeting sadness, you know? It’s this deep, pervasive despair. Like I was saying before about how it ruins everything outside of work... even if I'm just sitting on my couch trying to watch TV to turn my brain off—which never works, by the way, it never works—the TV is just meaningless background noise to this screaming in my head about how I'm failing everyone. The distress is just total. It's completely consuming. I don't know how else to describe it other than it feels like I'm mourning the loss of my own integrity while I'm still alive. 

I just... I can't escape it. I'll be in the middle of writing a note, and this wave of pure shame will wash over me so intensely that I feel sick to my stomach. It's this endless cycle of shame and terror, and it's so incredibly exhausting. I just feel so incredibly sad and terrified all the time. It’s just... it's too much. I really don't know how much longer a person can carry this much guilt before they just break entirely, you know? It’s just so unbelievably heavy.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being a bad doctor are something that you can consider as separate from your true self?

Separate from my true self? I... I really wish I could say yes to that. I mean, if I could just put these thoughts in a little box and say, "Oh, that's just the stress talking," or "That's just a symptom of being overworked," then maybe I could cope with it. But I can't. I can't separate them at all, because they don't feel like something outside of me. They feel like the absolute, fundamental truth about who I am. 

I know I brought this up a few minutes ago, but it really is the best way I can explain why it feels so completely inseparable from my core identity. It’s the charts. I will sit there at my desk, sometimes for hours, and I will review a patient's chart. And I can see with my own two eyes that there’s absolutely no evidence of a bad outcome. The data is right there in black and white—they are stable, they went home, their vitals are perfect. But it doesn't matter what the screen says. It just doesn't matter. I keep believing, with this terrifying, absolute certainty, that some routine delay on my part, or some slightly imperfect message I sent to the floor nurses, has quietly harmed them. 

It's not just a passing worry, it’s like... it's my reality. I am entirely convinced that this invisible damage is out there, and that everyone will eventually discover it. I just sit there picturing my associates, or the medical board, or the patients' families pulling the records and finally seeing exactly what I did, or what I didn't do quickly enough. They're going to see the quiet harm I've caused. 

When you believe something that strongly, when it completely overrides the objective facts right in front of your face... how do you separate that from your true self? It *is* my true self right now. It's the lens through which I see every single order I write, every patient I see, every breath I take in that clinic. I can't just step outside of it and look at it objectively, because the part of my brain that's supposed to be objective—the part that went to medical school and knows how to read a lab result—is the exact part that's telling me I'm a danger to these people. So, no, I... I can't separate it. I can't brush it off. It just feels like it's exactly who I am, and I don't know how to be anyone else anymore.
Are these thoughts affecting your personal relationships or daily activities outside of being a doctor?

Yeah, I mean, I know I touched on this a bit earlier when I said I was avoiding my residency buddies, but it really goes so much deeper than just hiding away because of the guilt. It's... it's like the entire color has been drained out of my life outside the clinic, and it's affecting all my daily activities and relationships in ways I never thought possible. 

I used to be the guy who organized everything for my friend group. Literally everything. Like, I would spend hours on Thursday nights plotting out these elaborate weekend hikes for everyone. I’d map out the exact trails, check the elevation gains, figure out the perfect timing so we could get to the summit right at dawn. I was huge into sunrise photography—I had this whole setup, all the heavy lenses, the tripod, the filters, and I’d drag everyone out of bed at 4 AM just to catch the perfect light hitting the trees. It was exhilarating, you know? I loved it. 

And if we weren't hiking, I was in the kitchen. I used to love cooking. I would spend all day Saturday driving around the city, sourcing ingredients from three different specialty markets just to make these massive, authentic Indonesian dinners for my friends. I'd make beef rendang that had to simmer on the stove for hours and hours, perfect nasi goreng, I'd even make the sambal completely from scratch. I loved the chaos of it, having ten or twelve people over, the house smelling like spices, everyone laughing... 

But now? For months now, just the thought of doing any of that... it just feels completely empty. It’s not just that I’m tired from work. It’s that I just... I don't care. I literally cannot make myself care about any of it anymore. My camera has been sitting in its bag gathering dust, and the idea of cooking a meal, even just for myself, let alone a big Indonesian feast, feels like climbing a mountain. When people reach out, those things just feel like these monumental, crushing obligations. I look at a text inviting me out, and I just feel... nothing. No excitement, no interest. Just this heavy dread about having to perform, having to pretend I care about the hike or the food or the conversation. All the things that used to make me who I am outside of medicine, they just feel like chores now that I can't even bring myself to start.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being a bad doctor are intrusive, meaning they enter your mind without you wanting them to?

Intrusive... I mean, when you use that word, intrusive, it makes it sound like... like a fly buzzing into a room through an open window, you know? Like something that absolutely doesn't belong there, something foreign that just suddenly pops into your head and you want to swat it away because it's annoying and out of place. But that's... that's really not how this feels at all. 

It's not like I'm sitting there having a perfectly normal day, feeling confident about my clinical judgment, and then out of nowhere this weird, random thought just barges in to ruin it. It's not an intrusion if it's already the entire foundation of the house, if that makes sense. I wouldn't say they enter my mind without me wanting them to, because it's really not about wanting or not wanting. It's just... it's just the reality of my situation. It's like... if you look outside and it's pouring rain. You don't have an "intrusive" thought that it's raining. You just see the rain, and you know it's raining, whether you actually want it to be raining or not. You're just observing a fact. 

That's exactly how my brain is operating with all of this. I'm not having these unwanted, random thoughts about being a danger to my patients... I'm just constantly, painfully aware of the fact that I am. It's just there. It's the baseline. Like, even yesterday, I was driving home from the clinic, and I had the radio on, just some local jazz station trying to... I don't know, distract myself for five minutes. And it wasn't like a thought suddenly intruded over the music. It's more like the music was just this incredibly thin, useless layer over this deep, ocean-level certainty that I had missed something critical on a patient's chart earlier that afternoon. 

So it's not an invader. It's just me. It's just my own brain processing what I believe is the absolute, undeniable truth about my incompetence. So, no, I really wouldn't call them intrusive. Honestly, I wish I could. If they were intrusive, maybe I could convince myself they were just... I don't know, mental glitches, you know? Just a misfire. But they aren't glitches. They're the entire operating system right now. It's just how I see reality.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being a bad doctor are in conflict with your own sense of identity and self-image?

Conflict? No... no, I wouldn't say it's a conflict. I think... I think my identity has completely morphed to just become this. I mean, honestly, the whole reason I'm even here talking to you today is because I feel, just so deeply, like I absolutely do not deserve the trust people put in me. 

You know how it is in this field. You walk into an exam room, you introduce yourself as the doctor, and patients just look at you with this immediate, unconditional faith. They hand over their health, they hand over their families, and they just trust you implicitly because of the letters after your name. And every single time they look at me like that, I just feel this crushing, suffocating weight because I know I don't deserve it. I feel entirely unworthy of it. 

It doesn't conflict with my self-image because my self-image right now is just... it's just that I'm a fraud. I will literally go home after a shift, sit on the edge of my bed in the dark, and I will just keep replaying these tiny, incredibly small clinical imperfections in my head. Like, maybe I took an extra minute to double-check a completely standard protocol, or maybe I didn't phrase a discharge instruction as eloquently as I could have, or I hesitated for half a second before answering a nurse's question. Just... incredibly small things that literally anyone else would forget by the time they walked down the hallway. 

But I can't forget them. I replay them on this endless, exhausting loop, dissecting every single second of the interaction, as if these minor moments are absolute, irrefutable proof that I am a dangerous doctor. I treat these little blips like they are smoking guns, like they are the ultimate evidence that I am quietly ruining people's lives. So, when you ask if it conflicts with who I am... no. It's exactly who I am now. I'm just someone who is dangerous, who doesn't deserve to be wearing that badge, and I just spend hours torturing myself, replaying the evidence of it over and over again.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being a bad doctor are something you wish you could stop thinking about?

Wish I could stop... honestly, no. I know that probably sounds completely backward to you. I mean, I'm sure anyone else sitting in this chair would probably be begging you for a pill to make it all go away, to just shut the noise off and get some peace. But for me... no. I don't wish I could stop thinking about it. 

Because if I stop thinking about it, what happens then? If I just, I don't know, let myself off the hook and go back to being oblivious... that’s when the real disaster happens. That's when someone actually gets hurt. I was thinking about this just the other night, actually. I was lying in bed, staring at the ceiling—it was maybe 2 or 3 in the morning, and the streetlights were casting these long shadows across the room—and I was just running through my patient list from the week, trying to find where I messed up. And for a split second, I was just so unbelievably exhausted, my brain just wanted to shut down and go to sleep. 

But then this sheer panic hit me. Because if I stop agonizing over every detail, if I stop hyper-fixating on my flaws and my mistakes... that means I'm getting complacent. And complacency in medicine is lethal. You know that, we both know that. If I'm not constantly on edge, constantly aware of how incompetent I am, I might miss something even bigger. 

So, as much as it hurts—and it does hurt, it's exhausting, it feels like I'm carrying lead weights around my ankles all day every day—I can't wish for it to stop. It feels like the only thing keeping my patients safe from me is the fact that I am constantly, obsessively monitoring how bad I am. If I let that go, if I just relax and stop thinking about it... I'd be negligent. I'd be a monster. So I feel like I *have* to think about it. It's my burden, sure, but it's also the only safeguard my patients have against me. I just... I can't afford to let my guard down for even a single second, so wishing for it to stop just feels incredibly selfish.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being a bad doctor are something that you dislike and want to get rid of, or are they more in line with how you actually feel about yourself?

Like I was trying to explain a minute ago, it's... it's absolutely in line with how I actually feel about myself. It's not some foreign object I want surgically removed or some annoying habit I want to break. I know I touched on this earlier, but it really bears repeating because it's the entire reason I'm here talking to you today... I just feel, down to my absolute core, that I do not deserve the trust people put in me. It's a fundamental truth about who I am now. 

When a patient looks at me, they see this competent professional, but I know I'm just playing a part. And that's why I keep replaying those small clinical imperfections I mentioned before. I'll just sit there, whether I'm driving or trying to eat dinner or trying to fall asleep, and I will comb through every single interaction, every chart I signed, every dosage I calculated. And even if it's just a tiny, insignificant thing—like a slight hesitation before answering a question or a slightly awkward phrasing during a physical exam—I replay it over and over as if these minor moments are definitive proof that I'm a dangerous doctor. 

So, to answer your question, no, I don't want to get rid of the thoughts. The thoughts aren't the problem. The problem is me. The problem is that I am completely unworthy of my medical license, and these thoughts are just the mirror showing me exactly how dangerous and inadequate I really am. Why would I want to smash the mirror just because I hate the reflection, you know? It wouldn't change the fact that I'm a risk to everyone I treat.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being a bad doctor are something that you would consider as inconsistent with your own self-image?

Doctor, I... I feel like maybe I'm just not explaining myself very well, because we keep kind of circling back to this exact same point. But no, it's not inconsistent at all. 

Like I've been trying to say, the whole reason I'm even sitting here in your office today is because I feel—just so fundamentally, down to my bones—like I do not deserve the trust people put in me. I know I've already brought up how I keep replaying those small clinical imperfections, but I really need you to understand *why* I do that. It's not because those thoughts feel foreign or out of character. It's because, to me, they act as undeniable proof that I'm a dangerous doctor. 

When I sit in the dark and obsess over a slightly awkward patient interaction or a minor charting delay, I'm not doing it because it clashes with my self-image. I'm doing it because it confirms everything I already believe about myself. It's like I'm a prosecutor building a legal case against myself every single day, gathering all these tiny pieces of evidence to prove how incompetent I am. 

So, no, there is no inconsistency. There's no conflict. If I looked in the mirror and thought, "Oh, this isn't me," that would be one thing. But I look in the mirror and think, "This is exactly who you are. You're a danger to your patients." It's just the reality of how I see myself right now, and I... I really don't know how else to articulate that to you without just repeating the exact same things all over again.
Do you feel like these thoughts about being a bad doctor are something that you believe are true about yourself, or do they feel like they are coming from outside of your own beliefs?

I... I feel like we are just having the exact same conversation on a loop here, Doctor. I really, truly do. I know I've said this like three times now, but I'll say it again, because maybe I'm just not using the right words. Yes, I believe they are true. They are entirely, one hundred percent coming from my own beliefs about myself. 

Like I said—and I really mean this, this is the whole reason I made this appointment and why I'm sitting here right now—I’m here because I feel like I don’t deserve the trust people put in me. That's not some outside force planting ideas in my head. That's me. That's my own assessment of my own failures. I keep replaying those small clinical imperfections I mentioned—the slight hesitations, the charting things, all of it—as if they prove I’m a dangerous doctor, because to me, they *do* prove it. They are the evidence that supports what I already know to be true about myself. 

I'm not sitting here thinking, "Oh, where did that thought come from? That's so unlike me!" I'm sitting here thinking, "Of course I messed that up, because I am fundamentally inadequate." It's coming from inside the house, so to speak. It's just... it's my reality. It's how I view my own competence, or lack thereof. I really don't know how else to explain that these thoughts are just a reflection of how completely worthless I feel as a physician. I'm not fighting them because they feel foreign; I'm drowning in them because they feel like the absolute truth.
Do you think there's any possibility that your belief about being a bad doctor might not be based in reality?

I hear what you're asking, I really do. You're asking if maybe my perspective is skewed, if this is all just... just in my head. But the thing is, it feels completely real to me, because of how it plays out in my day-to-day life. Let me try to explain it this way, because I spend hours—literally hours—doing this. 

I'll log into the electronic medical record system from home, usually late at night when I can't sleep, and I will pull up the charts of patients I saw days or even weeks ago. I will scour every single line. The vitals, the nursing notes, the lab trends, the discharge summaries, everything. And... and here is the thing. Even when I review the chart and there is absolutely no objective evidence of a bad outcome—like, the patient is stable, they went home, their labs normalized—I still sit there and I just *know* that I've done something terrible. 

I keep believing, with absolute, terrifying certainty, that some routine delay in my documentation, or some slightly imperfect message I passed along during sign-out, has quietly harmed that patient. It's not a passing worry or a 'what if.' It's a heavy, sinking fact in my chest. I look at a perfectly normal chart and I just think, well, the damage is already done, it's just hidden right now.
